claim: Natural sounds can be characterised by their spectral content and temporal modulation.
source: Natural sounds can be characterised by their spectral content and temporal modulation, but how the brain is organized to analyse these two critical sound dimensions remains uncertain.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about sound characteristics.

claim: There is a topographical representation of amplitude modulation rate in the auditory cortex of awake macaques.
source: Using functional magnetic resonance imaging, we demonstrate a topographical representation of amplitude modulation rate in the auditory cortex of awake macaques.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by fMRI data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The representation of temporal modulation rate is organized in approximately concentric bands of equal rates across the superior temporal plane in both hemispheres.
source: The representation of this temporal dimension is organized in approximately concentric bands of equal rates across the superior temporal plane in both hemispheres, progressing from high rates in the posterior core to low rates in the anterior core and lateral belt cortex.
evidence: This describes the spatial organization pattern observed in the fMRI data.

claim: High modulation rates are located in the posterior core of the auditory cortex.
source: The representation of this temporal dimension is organized in approximately concentric bands of equal rates across the superior temporal plane in both hemispheres, progressing from high rates in the posterior core to low rates in the anterior core and lateral belt cortex.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the fMRI data about the location of high rate preferences.

claim: Low modulation rates are located in the anterior core and lateral belt cortex.
source: The representation of this temporal dimension is organized in approximately concentric bands of equal rates across the superior temporal plane in both hemispheres, progressing from high rates in the posterior core to low rates in the anterior core and lateral belt cortex.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the fMRI data about the location of low rate preferences.

claim: In A1, the gradient of modulation rate runs approximately perpendicular to the axis of the tonotopic gradient.
source: In A1 the resulting gradient of modulation rate runs approximately perpendicular to the axis of the tonotopic gradient, suggesting an orthogonal organisation of spectral and temporal sound dimensions.
evidence: This describes the spatial relationship between two gradients observed in the data.

claim: There is an orthogonal organisation of spectral and temporal sound dimensions in A1.
source: In A1 the resulting gradient of modulation rate runs approximately perpendicular to the axis of the tonotopic gradient, suggesting an orthogonal organisation of spectral and temporal sound dimensions.
evidence: This is inferred from the perpendicular relationship of the gradients.

claim: In auditory belt areas, the relationship between spectral and temporal gradients is more complex than in A1.
source: In auditory belt areas this relationship is more complex.
evidence: This is a comparative observation from the data.

claim: There is a continuous representation of modulation rate across several physiological areas.
source: The data suggest a continuous representation of modulation rate across several physiological areas, in contradistinction to a separate representation of frequency within each area.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed data pattern.

claim: Frequency is represented separately within each auditory area.
source: The data suggest a continuous representation of modulation rate across several physiological areas, in contradistinction to a separate representation of frequency within each area.
evidence: This contrasts the organization of frequency representation with modulation rate representation.

claim: Tonotopy is a well-established organisational principle of the auditory system.
source: The topographical representation of frequency (tonotopy) is a well-established organisational principle of the auditory system.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge in auditory neuroscience.

claim: Tonotopy is established in the cochlea in mammals.
source: In mammals, tonotopy is established in the receptor organ, the cochlea, and maintained as a systematic spatial separation of different frequencies in different areas of the ascending auditory pathway, and in the auditory cortex.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about auditory system organization.

claim: Tonotopy is maintained as a systematic spatial separation of different frequencies in the ascending auditory pathway and auditory cortex.
source: In mammals, tonotopy is established in the receptor organ, the cochlea, and maintained as a systematic spatial separation of different frequencies in different areas of the ascending auditory pathway, and in the auditory cortex.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about auditory system organization.

claim: Temporal modulation is an essential perceptual component of communication sounds such as human speech and animal vocalisations.
source: While temporal modulation is recognised as an essential perceptual component of communication sounds such as human speech and animal vocalisations (Rosen, 1992; Drullman et al., 1994; Shannon et al., 1995; Wang, 2000; Chi et al., 2005; Elliott and Theunissen, 2009), its representation in the auditory system is poorly understood.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The representation of temporal modulation in the auditory system is poorly understood.
source: While temporal modulation is recognised as an essential perceptual component of communication sounds such as human speech and animal vocalisations (Rosen, 1992; Drullman et al., 1994; Shannon et al., 1995; Wang, 2000; Chi et al., 2005; Elliott and Theunissen, 2009), its representation in the auditory system is poorly understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Amplitude modulation rate is not spatially organised in the cochlea.
source: In contrast to sound frequency, amplitude modulation rate is not spatially organised in the cochlea but represented in the temporal dynamics of neuronal firing patterns.
evidence: This is established knowledge about how amplitude modulation is encoded in the cochlea.

claim: Amplitude modulation rate is represented in the temporal dynamics of neuronal firing patterns in the cochlea.
source: In contrast to sound frequency, amplitude modulation rate is not spatially organised in the cochlea but represented in the temporal dynamics of neuronal firing patterns.
evidence: This is established knowledge about how amplitude modulation is encoded.

claim: A considerable proportion of neurons in the auditory brainstem and cortex show tuning to amplitude modulation rates.
source: However, a considerable proportion of neurons in the auditory brainstem and cortex show tuning to amplitude modulation rates (reviewed in Joris et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Temporal information in sound is extracted by amplitude modulation filter banks.
source: It has been proposed that temporal information in sound is extracted by amplitude modulation filter banks (Dau et al., 1997a, 1997b) that are physiologically instantiated in the midbrain (Rees and Langner, 2005).
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal supported by citations.

claim: Amplitude modulation filter banks are physiologically instantiated in the midbrain.
source: It has been proposed that temporal information in sound is extracted by amplitude modulation filter banks (Dau et al., 1997a, 1997b) that are physiologically instantiated in the midbrain (Rees and Langner, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: At the stage of the inferior colliculus, amplitude modulation rate and frequency of sound are represented in approximately orthogonal topographical maps in rodents, cats, and primates.
source: Studies in rodents (Langner et al., 2002), cats (Schreiner and Langner, 1988) and primates (Baumann et al., 2011) have shown that at the stage of the inferior colliculus amplitude modulation rate and frequency of sound are represented in approximately orthogonal topographical maps.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies in multiple species.

claim: Whether the spatial organisation of amplitude modulation rate is preserved in the auditory cortex is debated.
source: Whether the spatial organisation of amplitude modulation rate is preserved in the auditory cortex remains is debated.
evidence: This describes the state of scientific debate in the field.

claim: Data from gerbils and cats suggest a topographical map for temporal modulation rates in the auditory cortex.
source: Data from gerbils (Schulze et al., 2002) and cats (Langner et al., 2009) suggest a topographical map for temporal modulation rates in the auditory cortex.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In cats, orthogonal gradients for modulation rate and frequency have been shown in the auditory cortex, similar to those in the inferior colliculus.
source: In cats, orthogonal gradients for modulation rate and frequency have been shown, similar to those in the inferior colliculus.
evidence: This is based on previous research in cats, implied from the context.

claim: It is not clear how orthogonal organization of modulation rate and frequency might be preserved across the multiple auditory fields of primate cortex where different fields show different orientations of the tonotopic gradient.
source: However, it is not clear how such an organisation might be preserved across the multiple auditory fields of primate cortex where different fields show different orientations of the tonotopic gradient.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Earlier fMRI studies in humans reported robust responses to a range of amplitude-modulated sounds, but no systematic organisation of rate.
source: While earlier fMRI studies in humans (Giraud et al., 2000; Schonwiesner and Zatorre, 2009; Overath et al., 2012) reported robust responses to a range of amplitude-modulated sounds, but no systematic organisation of rate, two more recent studies suggested an orthogonal relationship of frequency and rate in areas homologous to non-human primate auditory core (Herdener et al., 2013) and beyond (Barton et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous human fMRI studies.

claim: Two recent human fMRI studies suggested an orthogonal relationship of frequency and rate in areas homologous to non-human primate auditory core and beyond.
source: While earlier fMRI studies in humans (Giraud et al., 2000; Schonwiesner and Zatorre, 2009; Overath et al., 2012) reported robust responses to a range of amplitude-modulated sounds, but no systematic organisation of rate, two more recent studies suggested an orthogonal relationship of frequency and rate in areas homologous to non-human primate auditory core (Herdener et al., 2013) and beyond (Barton et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent human studies.

claim: Electrophysiology studies in non-human primates have shown tuning of individual neurons to different modulation rates.
source: Electrophysiology studies in non-human primates have shown tuning of individual neurons to different modulation rates and suggest a tendency for neurons in primary fields to prefer faster rates than neurons in field higher up the hierarchy (Bieser and Muller-Preuss, 1996; Liang et al., 2002): see also (Joris et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to electrophysiology studies.

claim: Neurons in primary auditory fields tend to prefer faster modulation rates than neurons in fields higher up the hierarchy.
source: Electrophysiology studies in non-human primates have shown tuning of individual neurons to different modulation rates and suggest a tendency for neurons in primary fields to prefer faster rates than neurons in field higher up the hierarchy (Bieser and Muller-Preuss, 1996; Liang et al., 2002): see also (Joris et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to electrophysiology studies.

claim: No clear topographical organisation of modulation rate across different auditory fields has been demonstrated in non-human primates prior to this study.
source: However, no clear topographical organisation of modulation rate across different auditory fields has been demonstrated in non-human primates.
evidence: This describes the state of knowledge before the current study.

claim: The study mapped the BOLD response to amplitude modulation rates from 0.5–512 Hz applied to a broad-band noise carrier in the auditory cortex of macaque monkeys.
source: In the current study we mapped the blood oxygen level dependent (BOLD) response to a wide range of amplitude modulation rates from 0.5–512 Hz applied to a broad-band noise carrier in the auditory cortex of macaque monkeys using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach of the study.

claim: The range of modulation rates from 0.5–512 Hz covers preferred rates for cortical neurons.
source: This range of modulation rates covers preferred rates for cortical neurons (Joris et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The topographic organisation of amplitude modulation rate in the macaque auditory cortex is arranged in concentric iso-rate bands.
source: The data reveal a topographic organisation of amplitude modulation rate in the macaque auditory cortex arranged in concentric iso-rate bands that are mirror-symmetric across both hemispheres with a preference for the highest rates in the postero-medial auditory cortex at the medial border of A1 and for the lowest rates in lateral and anterior fields.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the fMRI data.

claim: The concentric iso-rate bands are mirror-symmetric across both hemispheres.
source: The data reveal a topographic organisation of amplitude modulation rate in the macaque auditory cortex arranged in concentric iso-rate bands that are mirror-symmetric across both hemispheres with a preference for the highest rates in the postero-medial auditory cortex at the medial border of A1 and for the lowest rates in lateral and anterior fields.
evidence: This describes the symmetry pattern observed in the data.

claim: There is a preference for the highest modulation rates in the postero-medial auditory cortex at the medial border of A1.
source: The data reveal a topographic organisation of amplitude modulation rate in the macaque auditory cortex arranged in concentric iso-rate bands that are mirror-symmetric across both hemispheres with a preference for the highest rates in the postero-medial auditory cortex at the medial border of A1 and for the lowest rates in lateral and anterior fields.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the fMRI data.

claim: There is a preference for the lowest modulation rates in lateral and anterior auditory fields.
source: The data reveal a topographic organisation of amplitude modulation rate in the macaque auditory cortex arranged in concentric iso-rate bands that are mirror-symmetric across both hemispheres with a preference for the highest rates in the postero-medial auditory cortex at the medial border of A1 and for the lowest rates in lateral and anterior fields.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the fMRI data.

claim: The modulation rate gradient runs approximately orthogonal to the tonotopic gradients in the auditory core fields A1 and R.
source: This organisation results in a modulation rate gradient running approximately orthogonal to the tonotopic gradients in the auditory core fields, A1 and R.
evidence: This describes the spatial relationship observed in the data.

claim: The BOLD response was recorded to amplitude-modulated broad-band noise at six different rates (0.5, 2, 8, 32, 128, 512 Hz) across the auditory cortex of three monkeys.
source: In a first experiment we recorded the BOLD response to amplitude-modulated broad-band noise at six different rates (0.5, 2, 8, 32, 128, 512 Hz, see also [Baumann et al., 2011]) across the auditory cortex of three monkeys.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Two different maps were generated to reveal the spatial organisation of modulation rate: a contrast map and a best-rate map.
source: We generated two different maps to reveal the spatial organisation of modulation rate by projecting the data of the acquired volumes onto the cortical surface derived from the anatomical scans.
evidence: This describes the data analysis approach.

claim: The contrast map contrasted the response strength of the lower rate bands vs the higher rate bands.
source: In a first map (contrast map) we contrasted the response strength of the lower rate bands vs the higher rate bands to reveal the gradual change of preference for higher to lower modulation rates across the auditory cortex (Figure 1, top panels).
evidence: This describes the method for creating the contrast map.

claim: Data corresponding to the two highest rates (512 Hz, 128 Hz) and lowest rates (2 Hz, 0.5 Hz) were combined before contrasting in the contrast map.
source: The data corresponding to the two highest rates (512 Hz, 128 Hz) and lowest rates (2 Hz, 0.5 Hz) were combined before contrasting, while the intermediate rates were ignored (see also Baumann et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes the specific data processing method.

claim: In the best-rate map, the rate band that showed the strongest response was represented for each position in the auditory cortex.
source: In a second map (best-rate map), for each position in the auditory cortex, we represented the rate band that showed the strongest response.
evidence: This describes the method for creating the best-rate map.

claim: The contrast maps reveal preferences for high rates consistently clustered in the postero-medial auditory cortex with the maxima at the medial border of the primary field A1 in both hemispheres of all tested animals.
source: The contrast maps reveal a topography for different amplitude modulation rates with preferences for high rates consistently clustered in the postero-medial auditory cortex with the maxima at the medial border of the primary field A1 in both hemispheres of all tested animals.
evidence: This is a finding from the contrast map analysis.

claim: Preferences for low modulation rates were located lateral, anterior and to some degree posterior to the high-rate clusters.
source: Preferences for low rates were located lateral, anterior and to some degree posterior to the high-rate clusters.
evidence: This is a finding from the contrast map analysis.

claim: In the areas with the maximal preference for low or high rates, the contrast between low and high rates was statistically significant (p < 0.05) in all animals and hemispheres, corrected for multiple comparisons with family-wise error (FWE) correction.
source: In the areas with the maximal preference for low or high rates, the contrast between low and high rates was statistically significant (p < 0.05) in all animals and hemispheres, corrected for multiple comparisons with family-wise error (FWE) correction over the recorded volume.
evidence: This provides statistical support for the observed differences.

claim: The best-modulation-rate maps confirmed the systematic organisation of the response pattern with a topographic representation of rate arranged in approximately concentric frequency bands.
source: The best-modulation-rate maps for the six tested rates (Figure 1, bottom) confirmed the systematic organisation of the response pattern with a topographic representation of rate arranged in approximately concentric frequency bands starting with high rates in the postero-medial auditory cortex (at least a few voxels showed a best modulation rate of 128 Hz postero-medially in 5 of 6 hemispheres) and progressing anterior, lateral and in some cases posterior to lower rates (see also the schemata in Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the best-rate map analysis.

claim: At least a few voxels showed a best modulation rate of 128 Hz postero-medially in 5 of 6 hemispheres.
source: The best-modulation-rate maps for the six tested rates (Figure 1, bottom) confirmed the systematic organisation of the response pattern with a topographic representation of rate arranged in approximately concentric frequency bands starting with high rates in the postero-medial auditory cortex (at least a few voxels showed a best modulation rate of 128 Hz postero-medially in 5 of 6 hemispheres) and progressing anterior, lateral and in some cases posterior to lower rates (see also the schemata in Figure 4).
evidence: This is a specific quantitative finding from the data.

claim: The highest rate (512 Hz) was hardly represented in the best-rate maps.
source: The highest rate (512 Hz) was hardly represented in the best-rate maps.
evidence: This is an observation from the best-rate map analysis.

claim: The BOLD response was recorded to bandpass noise in three different frequency bands (0.5–1 kHz, 2–4 kHz, 8–16 kHz) in the same animals used in the first experiment.
source: In a second experiment, we recorded the BOLD response to bandpass noise in three different frequency bands (0.5–1 kHz, 2–4 kHz, 8–16 kHz) in the same animals used in the first experiment.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure for the frequency mapping experiment.

claim: Contrast maps and best frequency maps were generated for each animal in the frequency mapping experiment.
source: Based on these data, we generated contrast maps (Figure 2, top panels) and best frequency maps (Figure 2, bottom panels) for each animal similar to experiment 1.
evidence: This describes the data analysis approach for the frequency experiment.

claim: The frequency maps confirm the well-established tonotopic pattern with multiple reversals of the frequency gradient that serve as a basis for the delineation of auditory fields in the primate auditory cortex.
source: These maps confirm the well-established tonotopic pattern with multiple reversals of the frequency gradient that serve as a basis for the delineation of auditory fields in the primate auditory cortex (Morel et al., 1993; Kosaki et al., 1997; Petkov et al., 2006; Bendor and Wang, 2008; Baumann et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and confirmed by the current data.

claim: The findings from the frequency mapping experiment were confirmed using a 'phase-encoded' design in animals M1 and M2.
source: In a further experiment, we confirmed these findings using a 'phase-encoded' design (Sereno et al., 1995; Joly et al., 2014) in animal M1 and M2 (Figure 3).
evidence: This describes an additional validation experiment.

claim: Auditory fields were identified according to Hackett (2011), using procedures described in Petkov et al. (2006) and Baumann et al. (2010).
source: Based on these frequency maps, we identified auditory fields according to Hackett (2011), using procedures described in Petkov et al. (2006) and Baumann et al. (2010), adapted by the use of T1/T2 weighted MRI data to inform on the location of the core/belt border (Joly et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the method for identifying auditory fields, supported by citations.

claim: The anterior-posterior low to high frequency gradient that defines the auditory core field A1 is particularly clear in the contrast maps.
source: The anterior-posterior low to high gradient that defines the auditory core field A1 is particularly clear in the contrast maps (Figure 2, top panels).
evidence: This is an observation from the frequency contrast maps.

claim: The frequency gradient in A1 generally has a lateral-to-medial component in addition to the main anterior-posterior direction.
source: In line with previous studies in macaques, this gradient has generally a lateral-to-medial component in addition to the main anterior-posterior direction (Morel et al., 1993; Kosaki et al., 1997; Baumann et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by the current data and citations to previous studies.

claim: The low frequency area that defines the border between fields A1 and R is typically wider on the lateral side compared to the medial side.
source: Similar to the situation in humans, the low frequency area that defines the border between fields A1 and R is typically wider on the lateral side compared to the medial side.
evidence: This is an observation from the frequency maps.

claim: The anterior high frequency area, which forms the border between the auditory fields R and RT, is typically located on the medial side of the superior temporal plane, in the depth of the circular sulcus.
source: The anterior high frequency area, which forms the border between the auditory fields R and RT, is typically located on the medial side of the superior temporal plane, in the depth of the circular sulcus (see also Figure 4, Baumann et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an observation from the frequency maps, supported by a citation.

claim: The resulting anterio-medial direction of the main frequency gradient in R forms, in combination with gradient direction in A1, an inward inflection in the gradient axis across A1 and R.
source: The resulting anterio-medial direction of the main frequency gradient in R forms, in combination with gradient direction in A1, an inward inflection in the gradient axis across A1 and R, which has previously been reported in Morel et al. (1993) and Kosaki et al. (1997) in macaques, Bendor and Wang (2008) in marmosets and described in (Jones, 2003; Hackett, 2011; Baumann et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an observation from the current data, supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The directional change of the frequency gradient axis across the core fields is of particular relevance for the relationship of temporal and spectral gradients in these fields.
source: This directional change of the frequency gradient axis across the core fields, which is also obvious from the different mean angles of the gradients in A1 and R (Table 1), is of particular relevance for the relationship of temporal and spectral gradients in these fields (see Figure 4 and 'Discussion').
evidence: This is an interpretation of the significance of the observed gradient changes.

claim: The systematic, topographic representation of amplitude modulation rate extends over multiple fields to form a wider concentric organisation across the entire auditory cortex in both hemispheres.
source: The systematic, topographic representation of amplitude modulation rate we demonstrate extends over multiple fields to form a wider concentric organisation across the entire auditory cortex in both hemispheres.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding regarding the extent of the organization.

claim: In the auditory core areas (A1, R), the gradients for modulation rate and frequency lie approximately orthogonal to one another.
source: If this organization is overlaid with the spectral pattern derived from experiment 2, we notice that in the auditory core areas (A1, R) the gradients for modulation rate and frequency lie approximately orthogonal to one another (illustrated in schemata of Figure 4).
evidence: This is an observation from overlaying the two types of maps.

claim: The orthogonal arrangement of modulation rate and frequency gradients is most obvious in A1 in individual animals.
source: This arrangement is most obvious in A1 in individual animals, but the relationship generally holds for R and the adjacent lateral belt fields as well.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: The orthogonal relationship between modulation rate and frequency gradients generally holds for R and the adjacent lateral belt fields.
source: This arrangement is most obvious in A1 in individual animals, but the relationship generally holds for R and the adjacent lateral belt fields as well.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: The orthogonal arrangement occurs as a consequence of the change in the direction of the tonotopic axis between A1 and R.
source: This occurs as a consequence of the change in the direction of the tonotopic axis between A1 and R such that the tonotopic gradient follows approximately the iso- amplitude-modulation rate lines.
evidence: This is an explanation for the observed orthogonal relationship.

claim: The tonotopic gradient follows approximately the iso-amplitude-modulation rate lines.
source: This occurs as a consequence of the change in the direction of the tonotopic axis between A1 and R such that the tonotopic gradient follows approximately the iso- amplitude-modulation rate lines.
evidence: This describes the spatial relationship between the two gradients.

claim: The tonotopic axis runs anteriorly and medially in area R whilst the rate gradient runs anteriorly and laterally to preserve the orthogonal relationship.
source: In other words, the tonotopic axis runs anteriorly and medially in area R whilst the rate gradient runs anteriorly and laterally to preserve the orthogonal relationship.
evidence: This describes the specific directions of the gradients in area R.

claim: The frequency reversals form spokes in the concentric organisation of the amplitude modulation rate.
source: In this arrangement, the frequency reversals form spokes in the concentric organisation of the amplitude modulation rate (Figures 1, 2, 4 left).
evidence: This is a description of the spatial relationship between frequency reversals and rate organization.

claim: Rostral of R and caudal of A1, the orthogonality of spectral and temporal features breaks down and the gradients become more collinear and less obvious.
source: However, rostral of R and caudal of A1 the orthogonality of spectral and temporal features breaks down and the gradients become more collinear and less obvious (Figures 1, 2, 4 right).
evidence: This is an observation about the breakdown of orthogonality in certain regions.

claim: Gradient directions and relative orientations were calculated based on the contrast maps for the topographies of modulation rate and frequency in the auditory core fields A1 and R using a two dimensional regression analysis.
source: In order to quantify these observations we calculated gradient directions and relative orientations based on the contrast maps for the topographies of modulation rate and frequency in the auditory core fields A1 and R using a two dimensional regression analysis as described in Baumann et al. (2011).
evidence: This describes the quantitative analysis method.

claim: Relative gradients were calculated for the caudio-lateral field CL, representative for extra-core areas where the orthogonal direction breaks down.
source: We also calculated the relative gradients for the caudio-lateral field CL, representative for extra-core areas where the orthogonal direction breaks down.
evidence: This describes an additional analysis for comparison.

claim: All the calculated fields show a clear gradient.
source: All the calculated fields show a clear gradient.
evidence: This is a summary of the gradient analysis results.

claim: In A1, the gradient directions for rate and frequency clearly cross each other but deviate somewhat from perfect orthogonality with an average angle of 118.7 ± 22.3°.
source: In A1, the gradient directions for rate and frequency clearly cross each other but deviate somewhat from perfect orthogonality with an average angle of 118.7 ± 22.3°.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the gradient analysis.

claim: The calculated directions in field R are more variable, but also show an average relative angle for rate and frequency gradients of about 120° (117.2 ± 47.6°).
source: The calculated directions in field R are more variable, but also show an average relative angle for rate and frequency gradients of about 120° (117.2 ± 47.6°).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the gradient analysis.

claim: Relative angles in the postero-lateral field CL are much closer to anti-parallel with 4 of 6 hemispheres showing a relative angle around 160° and higher.
source: In contrast, relative angles in the postero-lateral field CL are much closer to anti-parallel with 4 of 6 hemispheres showing a relative angle around 160° and higher.
evidence: This is a quantitative result showing the breakdown of orthogonality in CL.

claim: This is the first demonstration of a systematic and topographic representation of amplitude modulation rate in the auditory cortex of non-human primates.
source: Here we demonstrate for the first time a systematic and topographic representation of amplitude modulation rate in the auditory cortex of non-human primates.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings.

claim: Concentric bands of decreasing modulation rates extend bilaterally from the medial auditory cortex in anterior, lateral and posterior directions.
source: Concentric bands of decreasing rates extend bilaterally from the medial auditory cortex in anterior, lateral and posterior directions.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding.

claim: In the region of the auditory core areas, the modulation gradients cross the well-established frequency gradients in approximately perpendicular direction leading to an orthogonal representation of the temporal and spectral dimensions of sound.
source: In the region of the auditory core areas, the modulation gradients cross the well-established frequency gradients in approximately perpendicular direction leading to an orthogonal representation of the temporal and spectral dimensions of sound.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding regarding orthogonality.

claim: The orthogonal organisation increasingly breaks down in extra-core auditory fields that tend to show a preference for slow rates.
source: This organisation increasingly breaks down in extra-core auditory fields that tend to show a preference for slow rates.
evidence: This is a summary of findings in extra-core areas.

claim: The topographical maps for temporal modulations are largely symmetrical across the hemispheres showing no signs of a consistent lateralisation for temporal features.
source: The topographical maps for temporal modulations are largely symmetrical across the hemispheres showing no signs of a consistent lateralisation for temporal features.
evidence: This is an observation about hemispheric symmetry in the data.

claim: The topographical representation of stimulus attributes is a common organising principle in the brain.
source: The topographical representation of stimulus attributes is a common organising principle in the brain.
evidence: This is general knowledge about brain organization.

claim: Topographical representation is found in the multiple retinotopic representations in the visual system and the somatotopic representations in the somato-sensory system.
source: Apart from sound frequency, we also find it in the multiple retinotopic representations in the visual system and the somatotopic representations in the somato-sensory system.
evidence: This is established knowledge about topographic organization in other sensory systems.

claim: Orthogonal representations of two topographic gradients have been previously demonstrated for other stimulus dimensions in the auditory system and the visual system.
source: Orthogonal representations of two topographic gradients have been previously demonstrated for other stimulus dimensions in the auditory system (Suga and O'Neill, 1979) and the visual system (e.g., Tootell et al., 1982; Sereno et al., 1995), and are predicted on theoretical considerations (Swindale, 2004; Watkins et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Orthogonal representations of two topographic gradients are predicted on theoretical considerations.
source: Orthogonal representations of two topographic gradients have been previously demonstrated for other stimulus dimensions in the auditory system (Suga and O'Neill, 1979) and the visual system (e.g., Tootell et al., 1982; Sereno et al., 1995), and are predicted on theoretical considerations (Swindale, 2004; Watkins et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: The partial orthogonal representation might facilitate the simultaneous analysis of different dimensions of sound.
source: In the current case the partial orthogonal representation might facilitate the simultaneous analysis of different dimensions of sound.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of the findings.

claim: Previous studies that investigated the representation of amplitude-modulation rate have not reported a topographical organisation of this temporal dimension in the auditory cortex.
source: Previous studies that investigated the representation of amplitude-modulation rate (Bieser and Muller-Preuss, 1996; Giraud et al., 2000; Bendor and Wang, 2008; Schonwiesner and Zatorre, 2009; Overath et al., 2012), have not reported a topographical organisation of this temporal dimension in the auditory cortex.
evidence: This is a statement about previous research, supported by citations.

claim: Electrophysiology studies in other primate species have highlighted a tendency for differential responses across different auditory fields with more primary areas preferring faster rates or showing shorter latencies and areas higher up the hierarchy preferring lower rates or showing longer latencies.
source: Electrophysiology studies in other primate species have highlighted a tendency for differential responses across different auditory fields with more primary areas preferring faster rates or showing shorter latencies and areas higher up the hierarchy preferring lower rates or showing longer latencies (Bieser and Muller-Preuss, 1996; Bendor and Wang, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous electrophysiology studies.

claim: Previous electrophysiology results have been interpreted in terms of a posterior-to-anterior high-to-low rate gradient or a core-to-belt high-to-low rate gradient.
source: These results have been interpreted in terms of a posterior-to-anterior high-to-low rate gradient (Bendor and Wang, 2008) or a core-to-belt high-to-low rate gradient (Camalier et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous interpretations.

claim: Both the posterior-to-anterior and core-to-belt gradient schemes have some merit, but they do not capture the full complexity of the organisation for temporal rates in concentric bands.
source: Given our results, both schemes have some merit, but they do not capture the full complexity of the organisation for temporal rates in concentric bands.
evidence: This is an interpretation comparing the current findings to previous interpretations.

claim: In addition to differential responses between fields, a clear gradient can be observed within the fields, particularly in the auditory core.
source: Furthermore, the maps for amplitude-modulation rate reported in this study (Figure 1) indicate that in addition to differential responses between fields a clear gradient can be observed within the fields, particularly in the auditory core.

claim: Two recent human fMRI studies reported a topographical gradient for amplitude modulation rate.
source: While earlier human fMRI studies (Giraud et al., 2000; Schonwiesner and Zatorre, 2009; Overath et al., 2012) did not show a clear topographical representation of amplitude modulation rate, two recent studies suggest a topographical gradient for this sound dimension (Barton et al., 2012; Herdener et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent human studies.

claim: Two recent human fMRI studies reported an orthogonal relationship of temporal rate and frequency in some auditory areas.
source: Furthermore, both studies reported an orthogonal relationship of temporal rate and frequency in some auditory areas.
evidence: This is supported by the cited human studies.

claim: The representation of modulation rates reported in Barton et al. (2012) in the human auditory cortex resembles the data from the current study with a maximal preference of high rates in the postero-medial cortex surrounded by areas with a preference for lower rates.
source: The representation of modulation rates reported in Barton et al. (2012) in the human auditory cortex resembles the data from the current study with a maximal preference of high rates in the postero-medial cortex surrounded by areas with a preference for lower rates.
evidence: This is a comparison between the current findings and a previous human study.

claim: The interpretation of the topographical pattern in Barton et al. (2012) differs from the current study, proposing a concentric organisation for frequency representation overlapping with an angular representation of modulation rate.
source: However, the interpretation of the topographical pattern of this study differs to ours, in proposing a concentric organisation for frequency representation overlapping with an angular representation of modulation rate in contrast to our interpretation of a concentric organisation for modulation rate and an angular representation of frequency in core areas.
evidence: This is a comparison of interpretations between studies.

claim: The current study interprets the organization as a concentric organisation for modulation rate and an angular representation of frequency in core areas.
source: However, the interpretation of the topographical pattern of this study differs to ours, in proposing a concentric organisation for frequency representation overlapping with an angular representation of modulation rate in contrast to our interpretation of a concentric organisation for modulation rate and an angular representation of frequency in core areas.
evidence: This is the interpretation of the current study's findings.

claim: Barton et al. (2012) suggested that each field contained a separate complete amplitude modulation rate gradient in addition to a separate and complete frequency gradient.
source: Furthermore, the study of Barton et al. suggested that each field contained a separate complete amplitude modulation rate gradient in addition to a separate and complete frequency gradient whilst the scheme that we demonstrate in macaques suggests that amplitude modulation rate is represented across multiple areas, none of which contain a complete map.
evidence: This is a description of the interpretation in Barton et al. (2012).

claim: The current study suggests that amplitude modulation rate is represented across multiple areas, none of which contain a complete map.
source: Furthermore, the study of Barton et al. suggested that each field contained a separate complete amplitude modulation rate gradient in addition to a separate and complete frequency gradient whilst the scheme that we demonstrate in macaques suggests that amplitude modulation rate is represented across multiple areas, none of which contain a complete map.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the current study's findings.

claim: A detailed comparison between the current study and Barton et al. (2012) is complicated by the use of a definition of the auditory fields that is incompatible with the definition commonly used in non-human primates.
source: However, a detailed comparison between the two studies is complicated by Barton et al. (2012), use of a definition of the auditory fields that is incompatible with the definition commonly used in non-human primates.
evidence: This is a methodological observation about comparing studies.

claim: The study by Herdener et al. (2013) focused on human homologues of the auditory core areas (hA1, hR) in the vicinity of the Heschl's gyrus.
source: The study by Herdener et al. (2013) focused on human homologues of the auditory core areas (hA1, hR) in the vicinity of the Heschl's gyrus.
evidence: This describes the focus of the Herdener et al. study.

source: The reported results in these areas are consistent with ours in that they suggest orthogonal relationships of frequency and amplitude modulation rates with similar gradient directions found to those in our study.
evidence: This is a comparison showing consistency between studies.

claim: A recent study in humans by Santoro et al. (2014) tested the representation of temporal and spectral features using a computational analysis approach.
source: Finally, a further recent study in humans tested the representation of temporal and spectral features (Santoro et al., 2014). The chosen approach differed from our and previous studies in that a computational analysis was applied to test different models of stimulus feature representation.
evidence: This describes the approach of the Santoro et al. study.

claim: Santoro et al. (2014) identified an area in postero-medial auditory cortex, just posterior of the medial Heschl's gyrus, with a preference for fast temporal rates.
source: Nevertheless, the study identified an area in postero-medial auditory cortex, just posterior of the medial Heschl's gyrus, with a preference for fast temporal rates.
evidence: This is a finding from the Santoro et al. study.

claim: In Santoro et al. (2014), regions anterior and lateral of the postero-medial area showed a preference for low temporal rates.
source: Regions anterior and lateral of this area showed a preference for low temporal rates (summarised in Figure 7 of Santoro et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from the Santoro et al. study.

claim: The pattern for temporal rate preference in Santoro et al. (2014) is consistent with the concentric pattern of rate representation observed in the current study.
source: Based on anatomical relationships in the auditory cortex between human and non-human primates as suggested in Baumann et al. (2013), such a pattern for temporal rate preference is consistent with the concentric pattern of rate representation observed here.
evidence: This is a comparison showing consistency between studies.

claim: Neuronal responses to modulation rate are usually divided into two different coding principles: rate coding and temporal coding.
source: In electrophysiology, neuronal responses to modulation rate are usually divided into two different coding principles: rate coding and temporal coding (e.g., Lu et al., 2001; Liang et al., 2002; Yin et al., 2011), reviewed in Joris et al. (2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge in electrophysiology, supported by citations.

claim: The rate code is a measure of the average number of spikes fired over a defined period of time to the different modulation rates.
source: The rate code is a measure of the average number of spikes fired over a defined period of time to the different modulation rates, and the temporal code is a measure of how well the neuron's firing synchronises with the amplitude envelope of the stimulus at different modulation rates.
evidence: This is a definition of rate coding in electrophysiology.

claim: The temporal code is a measure of how well the neuron's firing synchronises with the amplitude envelope of the stimulus at different modulation rates.
source: The rate code is a measure of the average number of spikes fired over a defined period of time to the different modulation rates, and the temporal code is a measure of how well the neuron's firing synchronises with the amplitude envelope of the stimulus at different modulation rates.
evidence: This is a definition of temporal coding in electrophysiology.

claim: The average response of neurons in the cortex shows slightly different best rates for rate code and temporal code measures.
source: The average response of neurons in the cortex shows slightly different best rates for the two measures and some neurons are properly tuned to only one of the two measures (Joris et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Some neurons are properly tuned to only one of the two coding measures (rate or temporal).
source: The average response of neurons in the cortex shows slightly different best rates for the two measures and some neurons are properly tuned to only one of the two measures (Joris et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Different neurons in the auditory cortex of non-human primates have been reported with tuning to modulation rates between 2–120 Hz, measured by temporal response and between 1–250 Hz measured by rate response.
source: Different neurons in the auditory cortex of non-human primates have been reported with tuning to modulation rates between 2–120 Hz, measured by temporal response and between 1–250 Hz measured by rate response (Bieser and Muller-Preuss, 1996; Liang et al., 2002), see also (Joris et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous electrophysiology studies.

claim: Neurons responding with a synchronised temporal response are rarely tuned to rates above 64 Hz and are preferentially located in primary areas.
source: However, neurons responding with a synchronised temporal response are rarely tuned to rates above 64 Hz and are preferentially located in primary areas.
evidence: This is based on previous electrophysiology research.

claim: Neurons demonstrating rate tuning make up the majority of neurons that respond to modulated sounds in non-primary auditory areas.
source: Neurons demonstrating rate tuning make up the majority of neurons that respond to modulated sounds in-non primary auditory areas and are frequently tuned to rates at 64 Hz and above.
evidence: This is based on previous electrophysiology research.

claim: Neurons demonstrating rate tuning are frequently tuned to rates at 64 Hz and above.
source: Neurons demonstrating rate tuning make up the majority of neurons that respond to modulated sounds in-non primary auditory areas and are frequently tuned to rates at 64 Hz and above.
evidence: This is based on previous electrophysiology research.

claim: It is not entirely clear which of the two response types (rate or temporal coding) are represented by the BOLD response reported in this study.
source: It is not entirely clear which of the two response types are represented by the BOLD response reported in this study.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of uncertainty in interpreting the BOLD signal.

claim: An increased average firing rate of a local sample of neurons to a certain modulation rate would lead to an increased BOLD response.
source: While an increased average firing rate of a local sample of neurons to a certain modulation rate would certainly lead to an increased BOLD response, an increased synchronisation within the same sample of neurons would probably have a similar effect.
evidence: This is based on understanding of the relationship between neural activity and BOLD signal.

claim: An increased synchronisation within a local sample of neurons would probably have a similar effect on BOLD response as increased firing rate.
source: While an increased average firing rate of a local sample of neurons to a certain modulation rate would certainly lead to an increased BOLD response, an increased synchronisation within the same sample of neurons would probably have a similar effect.
evidence: This is based on understanding of the relationship between neural activity and BOLD signal.

claim: A simulation study suggested that both rate and temporal coding firing patterns would influence the BOLD response in similar way.
source: This is supported by a simulation study which suggested that both types of firing patterns would influence the BOLD response in similar way (Chawla et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a simulation study.

claim: The range of amplitude-modulation rates represented in the BOLD response and the pattern of areas that respond to specific rates is better matched by response properties reported for single neurons responding with a rate code in non-human primates.
source: In our study, the range of amplitude-modulation rates represented in the BOLD response and the pattern of areas that respond to specific rates is better matched by response properties reported for single neurons responding with a rate code in non-human primates (Bieser and Muller-Preuss, 1996; Liang et al., 2002; Bendor and Wang, 2008).
evidence: This is a comparison between the current findings and previous electrophysiology studies.

claim: It is possible that the measured BOLD signal is a response to a combination of rate- and temporal-coding neurons.
source: Nevertheless, it is also possible that the measured BOLD signal is a response to a combination of rate- and temporal-coding neurons.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of what the BOLD signal might represent.

claim: The responses to different amplitude-modulation rates reported in this study are in line with results from previous electrophysiological studies in other non-human primates in the range of the preferred rates (2–128 Hz).
source: The responses to different amplitude-modulation rates reported in this study are in line with results from previous electrophysiological studies in other non-human primates (Bieser and Muller-Preuss, 1996; Liang et al., 2002) in the range of the preferred rates (2–128 Hz) as well as the preferred rates for the different fields.
evidence: This is a comparison showing consistency with previous studies.

claim: The current study showed the highest preference in A1 for a rate of 32 Hz and to a lesser extent to 8 Hz.
source: The current study showed the highest preference in A1 for a rate of 32 Hz and to a lesser extent to 8 Hz while similar electrophysiology studies in monkeys additionally highlighted 16 Hz, a rate not used in this study.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the current study.

claim: Similar electrophysiology studies in monkeys additionally highlighted 16 Hz as a preferred rate, a rate not used in this study.
source: The current study showed the highest preference in A1 for a rate of 32 Hz and to a lesser extent to 8 Hz while similar electrophysiology studies in monkeys additionally highlighted 16 Hz, a rate not used in this study.
evidence: This is a comparison with previous studies.

claim: Human studies showed slightly lower preferred rates between 2–8 Hz for primary areas while rates above 64 Hz were hardly represented.
source: Human studies (Giraud et al., 2000; Harms and Melcher, 2002; Overath et al., 2012) showed slightly lower preferred rates between 2–8 Hz for primary areas while rates above 64 Hz where hardly represented.
evidence: This is supported by citations to human studies.

claim: Species-specific values for preferred modulation rates are consistent with psychophysical comparisons between humans and macaques in an amplitude modulation discrimination task showing average peak sensitivities at lower rates in humans (10–60 Hz) than in macaques (30–120 Hz).
source: These species-specific values are consistent with psychophysical comparisons between humans and macaques in an amplitude modulation discrimination task showing average peak sensitivities at lower rates in humans (10–60 Hz) than in macaques (30–120 Hz) (O'Connor et al., 2010) or even a low-pass function in humans (Viemeister, 1979).
evidence: This is supported by citations to psychophysical studies.

claim: Different temporal response measures to different temporal stimulus features are highly correlated.
source: Various studies show however that different temporal response measures to different temporal stimulus features are highly correlated.
evidence: This is a general statement about temporal response measures.

source: Studies in the inferior colliculus showed good correlation of the representation of amplitude-modulation rate and the response latency of neurons in the inferior colliculus (Langner et al., 1987, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies in the inferior colliculus.

claim: Studies that recorded response latencies across different auditory fields showed a tendency for longer latencies in rostral fields.
source: Furthermore, studies that recorded response latencies across different auditory fields, showed a tendency for longer latencies in rostral fields (Bendor and Wang, 2008; Camalier et al., 2012) and belt fields (Camalier et al., 2012), consistent with the preference for slower modulation rates we found in these areas.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Studies that recorded response latencies across different auditory fields showed a tendency for longer latencies in belt fields.
source: Furthermore, studies that recorded response latencies across different auditory fields, showed a tendency for longer latencies in rostral fields (Bendor and Wang, 2008; Camalier et al., 2012) and belt fields (Camalier et al., 2012), consistent with the preference for slower modulation rates we found in these areas.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The tendency for longer latencies in rostral and belt fields is consistent with the preference for slower modulation rates found in these areas in the current study.
source: Furthermore, studies that recorded response latencies across different auditory fields, showed a tendency for longer latencies in rostral fields (Bendor and Wang, 2008; Camalier et al., 2012) and belt fields (Camalier et al., 2012), consistent with the preference for slower modulation rates we found in these areas.
evidence: This is a comparison showing consistency between the current findings and previous studies.

claim: Preferred amplitude-modulation rate is representative of the processing, or integration, time windows which characterise the time scale over which temporal features are integrated in a particular area or circuit.
source: This suggests that preferred amplitude-modulation rate is representative of the processing, or integration, time windows which characterise the time scale over which temporal features are integrated in a particular area or circuit.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional significance of modulation rate preferences.

claim: The systematic concentric organisation of amplitude-modulation rate could provide an anatomical basis for the analysis of different modulation rates in separate modulation filterbanks.
source: Here, we demonstrate a systematic, topographical representation of modulation rate in the auditory cortex of a non-human primate, organised, in parts, orthogonally to the established gradient for frequency. The systematic concentric organisation of amplitude-modulation rate that we demonstrate here, could provide an anatomical basis for the analysis of different modulation rates in separate modulation filterbanks (Dau et al., 1997a, 1997b).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of the findings, with citation to theoretical work.

claim: The superposition of maps of modulation rate and frequency also occurs in the inferior colliculus.
source: The superposition of maps of modulation rate and frequency also occurs in the inferior colliculus (Baumann et al., 2011) where some higher modulation rates are represented than in the cortex, whilst in the cortex the modulation rates mapped decrease with greater distance from A1.

claim: In the inferior colliculus, some higher modulation rates are represented than in the cortex.
source: The superposition of maps of modulation rate and frequency also occurs in the inferior colliculus (Baumann et al., 2011) where some higher modulation rates are represented than in the cortex, whilst in the cortex the modulation rates mapped decrease with greater distance from A1.
evidence: This is a comparison between the inferior colliculus and cortex, supported by a citation.

claim: In the cortex, the modulation rates mapped decrease with greater distance from A1.
source: The superposition of maps of modulation rate and frequency also occurs in the inferior colliculus (Baumann et al., 2011) where some higher modulation rates are represented than in the cortex, whilst in the cortex the modulation rates mapped decrease with greater distance from A1.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study.

claim: The mapping of distinct dimensions of sound, amplitude-modulation rate and frequency, as distinct vectors in an anatomical space, is analogous to the mapping of polar angle and eccentricity that occurs at all processing levels of the visual system.
source: The mapping of distinct dimensions of sound, amplitude-modulation rate and frequency, as distinct vectors in an anatomical space, is analogous to the mapping of polar angle and eccentricity that occurs at all processing levels of the visual system.
evidence: This is a comparison between auditory and visual system organization.

claim: Representation in the auditory cortex differs from the visual system in that a complete mapping of modulation rate does not occur within each cortical area.
source: Representation in the auditory cortex differs, however, in that a complete mapping of modulation rate does not occur within each cortical area, in contrast to the multiple and complete representations of spectral frequency that these areas contain.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the difference between auditory and visual system organization.

claim: Multiple and complete representations of spectral frequency occur within each auditory cortical area.
source: Representation in the auditory cortex differs, however, in that a complete mapping of modulation rate does not occur within each cortical area, in contrast to the multiple and complete representations of spectral frequency that these areas contain.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about tonotopic organization.
